Chapter 8. The Ripple Effect—How Forgotten Stories Shape the Present.
You know, it's so tempting to think of history as something set in stone—a bunch of facts locked away in the past, never changing. But if we look closer, the story of Ali shows us that's not really how it works. The past has a way of reaching into our lives, shaping how we see ourselves, and even the way we treat each other right now.
When local collaborators like Ali are erased from the record, it doesn't just twist the story of one expedition. It sets off a pattern—a ripple—that's still with us today.
Think about the way scientific discovery is usually taught. In classrooms and museums, it's almost always a line-up of so-called "great men"—one genius after another. But what about the local guides, the assistants, and the communities who made those discoveries possible? Their names are rarely mentioned. And that's not just a small mistake. It's a way of seeing the world that says some knowledge, and some people, just matter more than others.
Imagine a teacher, getting ready for a lesson on evolution. They flip through the textbook and see Wallace's name, but Ali's story is nowhere to be found. The students hear about the big ideas, the journeys, the discoveries—but not about the relationships and teamwork behind them. And this keeps happening, year after year, until it starts to feel normal. Inevitable, even.
But here's the good news: it doesn't have to stay this way. When we go back and recover those forgotten stories, something shifts. A museum curator might add a new label, finally giving credit to the local collectors. A scientist might pause, realizing just how much their own research depends on the work and wisdom of others. And maybe a student, hearing about Ali for the first time, starts to wonder—who else have we missed? What other stories are waiting to be heard?
That's the ripple effect in action. When we make the past more honest, we help make the present a little more just. Ali's story is a powerful reminder—history isn't just about what happened. It's about how we choose to remember, and those choices? They matter.
